heading: why geneva
subtitle: 46.2044° n, 6.1432° e
intro: we chose geneva because it felt like the right place to build a family. after living in london, geneva's plausibly the second most diverse european city in per capita terms — over 40% foreign residents, 180+ nationalities. and there's no equivalent of london's ethnic enclaves here. your kids grow up trilingual by accident, surrounded by families from everywhere, with the lake a bike ride away and the alps always in view.
why_here: kids spending their first years here seemed much better than anywhere else we'd lived or considered moving to. the city is compact enough to bike, safe enough for kids to roam, and ambitious enough — between cern, the humanitarians, investors, and third culture kids, you never run out of interesting people. the challenge for most people is to find a partner and a good job. both of these are locally solvable imho

sections.title: how high do you think the jet d'eau actually is?
sections.text: lake geneva is the collection of alpine water that defines the city. the magic is quotidian: sunrises by the quai in summer and sauna & lake plunge in winter. recent years have seen an impressive expansion of beach areas, restaurants & bars, plus free fitness and dance courses. everything is maintained in pristine condition and i haven't grown numb to living in a postcard after more than a decade here.
sections.caption: plage des eaux-vives, with the jet d'eau in the background

sections.title: international geneva
sections.text: geneva hosts countless international organizations, companies, ngos, research labs, and foundations. the city runs some of the most crucial international coordination and cross-cultural negotiations operations across business, science, and diplomacy. the density of altruistic, hard working individuals is unmatched. the main thing that's missing is a tinge of the 'tism and ambtion à la the bay area.
sections.caption: aerial view of the palais des nations

sections.title: diversity that actually mixes
sections.text: over 40% of geneva's residents are foreign nationals — and that's before counting dual citizens. french, portuguese, italian, spanish communities are the largest, but you'll find people from every continent. unlike london's patchwork of self-contained neighborhoods, geneva's small size forces mixing. the same café, the same tram, the same park. your kids' classmates come from 30 countries. it's cosmopolitan not as an aspiration but as a structural fact.
sections.caption: musiques en été at the ella fitzgerald stage, parc la grange

sections.title: precision & craft
sections.text: yes, patek philippe, rolex, vacheron constantin — they're all here. but the culture isn't flashy: the locals value precision, patience, and craft. that ethos seeps into everything: the trains run on time, the fondue is taken seriously, the public spaces well kept, and people show up when they say they will (+/- 15 minutes). the flashy things are usually owned by foreigners.
sections.caption: the movement of a patek philippe

sections.title: the alps next door
sections.text: on a clear day you can see mont blanc from the city center — the highest peak in western europe, only 80 kilometers away. skiing is an hour away. hiking starts at the city limits. the jura mountains offer gentler terrain and wilder solitude. natural beauty is the permanent frame around daily life. and we're finally starting to build higher buildings, too!
sections.caption: mont blanc seen from across the lake

closing: geneva doesn't try to sell itself. but if you value intellectual density, genuine diversity, natural beauty, and a place where kids can grow up with a wide aperture on the world — it's hard to beat. all you need is people to invite you to the non-public events. hit me up!
